description_full: PrimeEnergy Resources Corporation, through its subsidiaries, engages in acquisition, development, and production of oil and natural gas properties in the United States. The company owns leasehold, mineral, and royalty interests in producing and non-producing oil and gas properties; and operates wells and owns non-operating interests and royalties. It also acquires producing oil and gas properties through joint ventures with industry partners; and provides contract services to third parties, including well-servicing support operations, site-preparation, and construction services for oil and gas drilling and reworking operations. The company was formerly known as PrimeEnergy Corporation and changed its name to PrimeEnergy Resources Corporation in December 2018. PrimeEnergy Resources Corporation was incorporated in 1973 and is based in Houston, Texas.

financial_summary: PrimeEnergy Resources Corporati is a small-cap energy business with a $309M market cap on $189M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +15% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 21% against a 8% cost of capital — a 13-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $21M in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 3.68× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 13× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 4.4% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 60% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

ESG-driven capital flight and stranded asset risk — tightening climate policy and investor mandates raise the cost of capital and risk leaving reserves permanently in the ground.
Geopolitical supply shocks — wars, sanctions, and OPEC decisions create volatility that no hedging programme can fully neutralise.
